lessons.title: Closures: Capture Semantics & Escaping
lessons.body:
Closures capture the variables they reference, not a snapshot of their values — a captured `var` keeps referring to the same storage, so if that storage changes before the closure runs, the closure sees the new value.

```swift
var count = 0
let printCount = { print(count) }
count = 5
printCount() // prints 5, not 0
```

A capture list freezes a value at closure-creation time instead: `{ [count] in print(count) }` copies `count` into the closure's own storage right away, so a later mutation to the outer `count` doesn't change what the closure prints.

## Escaping vs non-escaping

A closure parameter is non-escaping by default: the compiler guarantees it's called before the function it's passed to returns, and that it's never stored anywhere else. Passing it to something asynchronous — storing it in a property, handing it to `DispatchQueue.main.async`, keeping it as a completion handler — requires marking the parameter `@escaping`, because the closure now needs to outlive the call.

```swift
func runLater(_ work: @escaping () -> Void) {
    DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 1, execute: work)
}
```

## Loops and per-iteration bindings

Each pass of a `for-in` loop introduces a fresh, independent binding for the loop variable, so closures created inside the loop body each capture their own iteration's value rather than one shared variable that keeps changing underneath them.

quickCheck.prompt: A function parameter's closure type is written without `@escaping`. What does that guarantee?
quickCheck.explanation: Non-escaping is the default for closure parameters: the compiler guarantees the closure is called before the function returns and isn't stored for later use, which is exactly what makes @escaping necessary for anything asynchronous.

options.text: The closure runs on a background queue
The closure is called before the function returns and isn't stored for later
The closure cannot capture any variables from its surrounding scope
The closure runs synchronously only if marked @Sendable

questions.prompt: You declare `struct Point { var x: Int }` at the top level of a file with no access modifiers written anywhere. What access level does `Point` get?
questions.explanation: Swift's default access level is `internal` when nothing is written — visible anywhere in the same module, but not to code outside it. That differs from `private` (scoped to the enclosing declaration) and from `public`/`open` (visible outside the module).

options.text: public
private
internal
fileprivate

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Arrays are value types with copy-on-write: assigning `counters` to `copy` doesn't copy the buffer immediately, but mutating `copy` through a subscript triggers the copy first, so `counters` keeps its own independent storage and its first element is left untouched.

codeSnippet.code:
struct Counter {
    var value = 0
}

var counters = [Counter(), Counter()]
var copy = counters
copy[0].value = 99
print(counters[0].value)

options.text: A compile error, since copy[0].value can't be assigned through a subscript on an array of a custom struct without an explicit setter
nil

questions.prompt: You write `let box = Box()`, where `Box` is a class with a mutable stored property `count`. Which statement about `box.count += 1` is accurate?
questions.explanation: `let` only fixes the variable `box` itself — it can't later be reassigned to point at a different instance. The instance it refers to is still a reference type with mutable stored properties, so mutating `count` through it compiles and works fine.

options.text: box.count can't be mutated, since let applied to a class instance makes every one of its stored properties immutable for the lifetime of the variable
box can later be reassigned to point at an entirely different Box instance, since let restricts only the instance's internal stored properties rather than the variable binding itself
Box must redeclare count as a let constant too, or the code is rejected at compile time before box.count += 1 can ever run
box itself can't be reassigned to a different instance, but count and its other stored properties can still be mutated through it

questions.prompt: Given `let length = user?.address?.city?.count`, if `user.address` is nil, what is `length`?
questions.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits at the first nil link and produces nil for the whole expression, typed as an Optional of whatever the final property's type would have been — here, `Int?`.

options.text: nil, typed as Int?
A runtime crash, since chaining through a nil optional force-unwraps every intermediate link along the way
An empty string, since count on a nil chain defaults to a zero-length String before being converted to a count

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `compactMap` applies the closure to every element and drops any nil results from the output, so the four non-nil values [1, 2, 4, 6] remain — a count of 4.

options.text: nil

questions.prompt: A view controller sets `networkClient.onComplete = { self.updateUI() }` inside `viewDidLoad`. Compare that to writing `{ [weak self] in self?.updateUI() }` instead.
questions.explanation: The plain closure captures `self` strongly; if `networkClient` is retained by `self` (directly or indirectly) and holds onto the closure, that's a reference cycle — neither object can deallocate. `[weak self]` breaks the cycle by capturing an optional, weak reference instead, letting self deallocate normally while the closure safely no-ops if it's already gone.

options.text: They behave identically at runtime; [weak self] is purely a style preference with no effect on memory
The plain closure is safer, since capturing self strongly guarantees that updateUI() always has a valid, fully initialized instance available to call no matter when the closure eventually runs
[weak self] makes updateUI() run on a background queue instead of the main thread
The plain closure risks a retain cycle if self indirectly retains the closure; [weak self] avoids it by capturing self as an optional, weak reference

questions.explanation: Methods on a struct don't implicitly get write access to `self`'s stored properties, since structs are value types and a plain method might be called on a `let` instance; marking the method `mutating` opts in explicitly, and the compiler then rejects calling it on a `let` instance.

options.text: func declarations can't reference stored properties at all in Swift
By default, a struct's instance methods can't modify its stored properties — mutating opts in to that
value would need to be declared as an optional (var value: Int?) instead of a plain Int, since only optional stored properties are mutable from within a struct's own instance methods
increment() would need to be marked static to change value

questions.prompt: How would you best describe an enum case declared as `case success(User)` alongside `case failure(Error)`?
questions.explanation: Associated values let each case carry its own typed payload — here, the enum can be pattern-matched to extract either the wrapped User or the wrapped Error, rather than needing a separate class hierarchy or a struct with optional fields where at most one is ever non-nil.

options.text: A case with a payload: pattern matching can extract the associated User or Error value specific to whichever case matched
A computed property that returns either a User or an Error depending on context
A protocol requirement that any conforming type must implement
A struct with two optional properties, user and error, where exactly one of them is always non-nil while the other stays nil for the lifetime of the value

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `defer` blocks run in reverse order of registration, right before the enclosing scope exits — after both prints execute, the second defer (registered last) runs first, then the first defer (registered first, but last to run) runs after it.

options.text: start, end, cleanup, second defer
cleanup, second defer, start, end
start, end, second defer, cleanup
start, cleanup, end, second defer

questions.prompt: How is throwing `func fetch() throws -> User` different from returning `func fetch() -> Result<User, Error>`, from a caller's perspective?
questions.explanation: A throwing function propagates failure via Swift's error-propagation mechanism — the caller must try/catch it or propagate it further with throws — while Result reifies success or failure as an ordinary value that can be stored, passed around, or handled later without try at all.

options.text: They're identical; Swift automatically converts one form into the other wherever they appear
Result can only be used inside async functions, while throws works everywhere
throws is always faster at runtime than Result, since Result boxes its payload on the heap regardless of whether User and Error are small value types that would otherwise fit inline
throws requires the caller to use try/catch (or propagate with throws); Result is a plain value that can be stored, passed around, and inspected without try at all

questions.prompt: You have `enum Direction { case north, south, east, west }` and a `switch` over a `Direction` with a case for each of the four, and no `default`. What happens if a fifth case, `case up`, is added to the enum later?
questions.explanation: Swift's switch statements over an enum must be exhaustive; adding a new case without a matching switch case (and no default) is a compile error everywhere that enum is switched over — which is the point, since it surfaces every place that needs updating instead of silently doing nothing for the new case.

options.text: Nothing — the switch still compiles and up is simply never matched at runtime
Every switch over Direction that isn't exhaustive (and has no default) now fails to compile, flagging the missing case
The compiler inserts an implicit default: break automatically for the new case
The program compiles fine either way, but crashes at runtime the very first time a Direction.up value is actually passed into this particular switch statement

questions.explanation: A `guard`'s `else` branch must leave the enclosing scope — with `return`, `break`, `continue`, or a call to a function that never returns — because the whole point of `guard let` is that `n` is guaranteed to exist for the rest of the scope. Without an exit, the compiler can't guarantee that, so it rejects the code.

options.text: The else branch doesn't exit the scope (e.g. with return), so the compiler can't guarantee n exists afterward
guard only supports plain Bool conditions in every version of Swift, and never supports optional binding with let inside its condition clause
name must be a non-optional String for guard let to apply
print inside an else branch isn't allowed in Swift

questions.prompt: You store items in a `Set<String>` instead of an `Array<String>` to remove duplicates. What must be true of the element type for this to work, and what do you give up?
questions.explanation: Set requires its element type to conform to Hashable (String already does) so it can bucket elements for fast membership checks and de-duplication; in exchange, a Set has no defined ordering, so iterating it doesn't reproduce the order elements were inserted in.

options.text: The element type must conform to Comparable, and you give up the ability to check membership in O(1)
Nothing needs to change, and Set preserves insertion order just like Array does
The element type must conform to Hashable, and you give up insertion-order iteration
The element type must conform to Codable so it can be archived to disk automatically, and you give up the ability to ever store duplicate values in the collection at all

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `didSet` only fires on an assignment made after the property already has a value from initialization — it doesn't run for the default value set while the instance is being constructed. Setting `temperature = 72` afterward does trigger it, printing the old and new values.

options.text: changed from 70 to 70, then changed from 70 to 72 — didSet also fires once for the default value assigned during initialization
Nothing prints, since didSet never fires on a struct's stored property, only ever on a class's
changed from 0 to 72, since oldValue always defaults to 0 the very first time didSet runs for any property
changed from 70 to 72

questions.prompt: Two extensions of the same struct live in the same file, and a method in one extension needs to call a private helper declared in the other extension. Does that work with `private`, or does it require `fileprivate`?
questions.explanation: `private` is visible from any extension of the same type within the same file, not just the exact declaration it's written in — so this already works with `private`. `fileprivate` would only be necessary if the caller lived in a different type, or in a top-level function, in the same file.

options.text: Neither — cross-extension calls to a private helper always require making it internal instead
private already covers this — it's visible across all extensions of the same type in the same file
Only fileprivate works here, since private is scoped strictly to the single individual extension block where it happens to be declared, never anything wider
It requires public, since extensions are compiled as if they were separate modules

questions.prompt: A function stores a completion closure onto a property to call later, after the function itself has already returned: `func load(completion: @escaping (Data) -> Void)`. Why is `@escaping` required here?
questions.explanation: Closure parameters are non-escaping by default, meaning the compiler guarantees they're called before the function returns and never persist past that call. Storing the closure in a property means it will outlive the function call, which the compiler only allows if the parameter is explicitly marked @escaping.

options.text: Because the closure is stored for later use and will outlive the function call, which non-escaping closures aren't allowed to do
Because Data isn't a value type, and only value-typed closures can be non-escaping
Because completion handlers always need to run on a background queue somewhere, and only closures marked @escaping are capable of running off the main thread at all
Because the function is async, and only async functions can accept closure parameters at all

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Each pass of a for-in loop introduces a fresh, independent constant for the loop variable, so every closure captures its own iteration's value of i rather than one shared variable that keeps changing underneath them — the classic 'every closure prints the last value' bug from languages with a single mutable loop variable doesn't happen here.

options.text: 3, 3, 3 — every closure shares the same i, which has finished looping by the time they run
A compile error, since i can't be captured inside a for-in loop's body without an explicit capture list
0, 1, 2 — each iteration captures its own independent value of i
2, 1, 0, since closures capture and replay values in reverse order of insertion

questions.prompt: A struct's stored properties are all Codable, and you add a custom CodingKeys enum that omits one of them — a property that has a default value. What happens to automatic Codable conformance?
questions.explanation: Swift still synthesizes `init(from:)` and `encode(to:)` from CodingKeys, but only the cases listed in the enum participate in coding — a property left out of CodingKeys is simply skipped by both encoding and decoding, which only compiles because that property has a default value the synthesized initializer can fall back on.

options.text: Synthesis stops entirely, and you must write encode(to:) and init(from:) by hand
The omitted property is encoded anyway, since CodingKeys only affects decoding, never encoding
A compile error occurs, since CodingKeys requires listing every single stored property, and the synthesized initializer rejects any enum that omits one
Synthesis still works, but the omitted property is skipped entirely by both encoding and decoding

questions.prompt: Why does this fail to compile?
questions.explanation: `static` members are implicitly final — they can't be overridden by a subclass at all. Overriding a type-level method in a subclass requires declaring it `class func` in the base class instead, which explicitly permits subclasses to override it.

options.text: describe() needs to be marked @objc for the subclass to override it
static implies final; Dog would need Animal to declare describe() as class func instead to override it
Dog can't override any method declared in Animal without also overriding init
override is only valid for instance methods, and static func describe() is a computed property in disguise

questions.prompt: A class has `lazy var config: Config = loadConfigFromDisk()`. Two different properties on the same instance each read `config` before anything else touches it. How many times does `loadConfigFromDisk()` run?
questions.explanation: `lazy` defers initialization until the first access, then caches the result — every later read returns the already-computed value without calling the initializer expression again, so it runs exactly once no matter how many properties or call sites read it afterward.

options.text: Once — the first access computes and caches it; later reads just return the cached value
Twice — once per property that reads it
Zero times, since lazy properties are only ever evaluated when explicitly forced with a separate call to config.evaluate()
Every time config is read, since lazy only defers the type declaration, never the actual evaluation of the initializer expression itself

questions.prompt: Given `struct User { var name: String }` and `let users: [User]`, what does `users.map(\.name)` do, compared to `users.map { $0.name }`?
questions.explanation: `\.name` is a key path literal — used here where a `(User) -> String` function is expected, which Swift converts automatically. It produces exactly the same `[String]` result as the closure form; the difference is spelling, not behavior.

options.text: It fails to compile, since map only ever accepts closures, never key paths, as an argument
It returns the User instances unchanged, since \.name is treated as a filter predicate rather than a transform
It returns the same [String] array of names as the closure form — a key path used where a function is expected
It returns an array of key paths instead, one full KeyPath<User, String> value per element, rather than ever unwrapping to the underlying String values themselves

questions.prompt: A function `func parse(_ s: String) throws -> Int` is called as `let value = try? parse(input)`. What is the type of `value`, and what happens if `parse` throws?
questions.explanation: `try?` converts a throwing call into an Optional: if the call succeeds, `value` is `.some(result)`; if it throws, the specific error is discarded and `value` is simply `nil` — an `Int?`, not an `Int` or a `Result`.

options.text: value is still plain Int, and any thrown error automatically propagates further up to the caller's own caller instead
value is Result<Int, Error>, capturing whichever case actually applies
value is Int, and a thrown error is silently replaced with 0
value is Int?, and a thrown error becomes nil, discarding the specific error

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Swift's String.count counts extended grapheme clusters — user-perceived characters — not Unicode scalars. Two Regional Indicator scalars combine into a single grapheme cluster (a flag emoji), so count is 1 even though the string is built from two separate Unicode scalar values.

codeSnippet.code:
let flag = "\u{1F1FA}\u{1F1F8}" // built from two Regional Indicator scalars
print(flag.count)

options.text: 2, since count reports the number of Unicode scalar values that make up the string
1 — the two scalars combine into a single extended grapheme cluster
4, since count reports UTF-8 code units for characters outside the ASCII range
0, since emoji aren't considered valid Character values in a Swift String

questions.prompt: You write `func firstMatch<C: Collection>(in collection: C, equalTo target: C.Element) -> C.Element? where C.Element: Equatable`. Why is the `where` clause needed, given that `Collection` already appears as a constraint?
questions.explanation: `Collection` by itself says nothing about whether its `Element` associated type supports `==` — that's a separate capability. The `where C.Element: Equatable` clause adds that requirement on the associated type specifically, which is what lets the function body compare elements with `==`.

options.text: Collection alone doesn't guarantee its Element is Equatable; the where clause adds that separate requirement on the associated type
Without it, the function fails to compile for a different reason — generic functions always require at least two separate constraints listed together before they're considered valid
The where clause is only decorative here; Collection already implies Equatable elements in every case
It restricts C itself to arrays, since where clauses on associated types only ever apply when C happens to be Array

questions.prompt: A function is declared `func makeShape() -> some Drawable`. Can two different calls to `makeShape()` return values of two different concrete types, both conforming to Drawable?
questions.explanation: `some Drawable` (an opaque return type) commits the function to one single concrete type, chosen once by the function's own implementation — every call returns that same underlying type, even though callers only ever see it as Drawable. Returning `any Drawable` instead would allow a different concrete type per call, at the cost of type-erasing every value.

options.text: Yes — some Drawable means each call is free to return a different concrete type, so long as it conforms
No, because Drawable itself would need to be declared as a class-only protocol before any opaque return type involving it could be considered valid
No — some commits the function to one single concrete type for all calls; any Drawable would be needed to vary it per call
Yes, but only if Drawable has no associated types or Self requirements anywhere in its definition

questions.prompt: Given this property wrapper, what is the type and meaning of `$health` when accessed on a Player instance?
questions.explanation: The `$` prefix accesses a property wrapper's `projectedValue`, whatever type that's declared as — here it's `Bool`, defined to mean 'value is at the top of its clamped range,' not the health value itself. `health` (no `$`) still goes through `wrappedValue`, the clamped Int.

options.text: Int, the same clamped value as health itself, just accessed through a different spelling
ClosedRange<Int>, the range health is clamped to
A compile error occurs here, since $ -prefixed access is only ever meaningful on properties wrapped specifically with Combine's @Published, never a custom property wrapper
Bool, defined by projectedValue here as whether health is currently at the top of its clamped range

questions.prompt: Why can't you add a new stored property to a type through an extension, the way you can add a computed property or a method?
questions.explanation: Extensions can't change a type's memory layout. A stored property needs space allocated for it at the point an instance is created, but an extension is compiled separately from — and often after — the original declaration, with no way to retroactively resize every existing instance of that type.

options.text: Stored properties require the @objc attribute, which extensions can't apply to a type they don't originally declare
A stored property needs space in the type's memory layout, and extensions can't retroactively change that layout
Extensions can only be applied to protocols, not to concrete structs or classes, so stored properties never apply
It's a language limitation planned for removal — a future Swift version will allow stored properties in extensions
